description: We are Project: Hail Mary, a team from Ecuador passionate about science, technology, and innovation. We are participating in the NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026 to develop a solution that integrates MODIS and VIIRS satellite data to analyze and visualize thermal hotspots. Our interests include programming, data analysis, visualization, and remote sensing to address real-world challenges.
summary:
Hail Mary is an interactive atlas of recorded thermal activity around mainland Ecuador from January 2003 through October 2026. Using NASA FIRMS data from MODIS and Suomi NPP VIIRS, it addresses a key challenge: sensors detect thermal activity differently, making their historical records difficult to compare directly.

We developed an exploratory MODIS-equivalent index and a visual calendar where users can select an area, compare months across years, explore historical high-activity seasons and export results. Original sensor records, sources and limitations remain visible alongside the adjusted values.

A comparison with MODIS over 2023–2025 helps users assess the adjustment and its limitations. The project supports students and analysts in investigating historical patterns while distinguishing sensor differences from changes in recorded activity. It does not predict fires, count individual fires or measure burned area. Observation coverage and accuracy in individual areas remain unverified.
details:
Hail Mary helps users investigate how recorded thermal activity varies across months and years while making differences between satellite sensors visible.

NASA FIRMS MODIS and Suomi NPP VIIRS detections are aggregated into 0.05-degree grid cells and mainland Ecuador local days (UTC−5). Each sensor contributes one active cell-day when a cell contains at least one accepted detection on a date. The exploratory index H uses observed MODIS through 2022 and monthly-adjusted VIIRS from January 2023.

We fitted three adjustment candidates using February 2012–December 2018 and selected monthly factors using national comparisons for 2019–2022. A later comparison across 36 months in 2023–2025 produced a mean absolute difference of 34.871 active cell-days per month, equivalent to 21.27% of mean observed MODIS activity. This is a comparison between sensors, not validation against ground truth. Agreement weakened in 2025: December adjusted VIIRS activity was 1,219.208 MODIS-equivalent active cell-days versus 678 observed MODIS active cell-days. We did not quantify the contribution of orbital drift.

The interface offers an area selector, monthly magnitude and retrospective anomaly calendars, historical seasonal windows, sensor-comparison charts and CSV exports. Anomaly ranks compare a month with the same calendar month in other eligible years. The seasonal window captures at least 70% of the sum of twelve monthly medians. For the full study grid, October–December captures 77.595% of that profile.

The Python pipeline and React/TypeScript frontend preserve source information, units, archive availability and limitations. Vite builds the static application; MapLibre and OpenFreeMap provide the optional map. GitHub Pages hosts the project.

Our contribution is a traceable connection between original observations, sensor adjustment and an accessible historical calendar. Students and analysts can explore patterns without treating raw detection counts from different sensors as directly interchangeable. Impact on users has not yet been measured.

The study rectangle includes neighboring territory. National factors do not establish local accuracy. Satellite observation coverage remains unverified, historical MODIS collection identity has unresolved provenance questions, and 2026 includes provisional near-real-time inputs. Recorded zeros do not prove absence of fire. H is neither a count of individual fires nor burned area, a forecast or a safety assessment.
